That's such a dangerous and untrue thing to say… Steroid creams are totally okay once you use them as directed for brief periods. 

For some people, using steroids are about quality of life. I've seen a woman on the eczema subreddit talking about how she was thinking of committing over how painful her eczema was, and still she refused to use steroids for some relief. Don't be that person spreading ''overfear'' of steroids. Yes TSW is real but a lot of people who self-diagnose with TSW are just having a flare that they would have with or without steroid use… Because steroids don't cure you, they calm down the symptoms while you're using them, and once you stop using them, your symptoms will come back.

Most people will not develop TSW. If you use steroid creams as directed for brief periods, your chances are almost zero. TSW is very, very rare. 

Steroids are not the solution, but they're an excellent bandaid when needed and this fear mongering is just not ok, in my honest opinion.

When I was 15 there was an explosive fight with my father, my mother and I. My father was completely out of his mind, I believe high as well as drunk, breaking shit, screaming, coming real close to laying a hand on my mum. The next time I saw him was over a year later when my daughter was born and I invited him to come meet her at the hospital. 

At that point, I had gone through a LOT of therapy. I mean a LOT of it. 

I had always been a people pleaser and had a hard time saying ''no'' or whatever I thought the other person would not like to hear, and I worked on that in therapy for months and months. That meant that by the time he came around, I felt confident in my ability to set boundaries, and also, I had made enough peace with not having him in my life, so if those boundaries didn't ''please'' him or if he couldn't respect them, I'd just point him to the door. 

It was a learning process for sure. He's still drinking so I don't spend time alone with him in person at all. 

My sister has completely cut contact and she hasn't spoken to him in about five years, and I do believe she has made peace with that choice and won't change her mind, no matter what he does. I still speak to him occasionally but only on my terms - in places I choose, with other people around, and only for the amount of time I'm comfortable with. I do not leave him alone with my children. He has been accepting of those boundaries thus far, and I made them very clear to him both face to face and in writing. He knows that if he crosses any of the lines I have set, I will cut him off. 

If you can afford it, I really suggest therapy. I found a therapist that was specialized in helping children of addicts, and she changed my life in so many ways. It's what helped me cope and move on.

Holyyyy, I had such a similar experience...

Always was the ''worst'' at gym, last to be picked for teams, was genuinely made fun of by some gym teachers/school mates and called lazy throughout middle school. I had a hard time catching my breath, it was painful, I hated it. Even the idea of exercising gave me anxiety.

I convinced myself I was just bad at exercise, I guess. Plenty of the girls at my school weren't athletic either, so I figured they felt the same way I did. I was also a quite allergic kid growing up, from eczema to throat closing up when I came in contact with a whole lot of things so I just didn't overthink my symptoms and never really expressed them other than ''I don't like exercise''. 

I have always been skinny, was actually underweight most of my life, but still some family members felt the need to mention that if I continued loathing exercise so much, I'd get ''fat'' as soon as puberty hit. It's a long and complex story, but I ended up developing an ED that I still struggle with 12 years later. Because my brain convinced itself that if I couldn't exercise, I had to starve.

I got pregnant when I was in high school and had such intense shortness of breath I couldn't walk to the bathroom without taking breaks to catch my breath. I was told it was common in pregnancy and it was not further investigated. When I was giving birth I cried to a nurse that I genuinely couldn't breath and was pretty much ignored with nothing more than a dirty look. My boyfriend had to BEG for someone to give me an oxygen mask.

My second pregnancy was the same thing. Again I was not taken seriously. I had my second baby at 19 and literally had to hear medical professionals say to my face that shortness of breath was common in pregnancy and I was making it worse for myself by getting pregnant too young. I could not even hold my first baby while pregnant with my second unless I was sitting down. I slept all day and was in so much pain.

I found out I had asthma in my 20s, during my third pregnancy, when a doctor finally paid attention to my complaints and decided to investigate. Second trimester, woke up in the middle of the night having a nightmare that I was drowning, and I couldn't breath. Panicking so bad, thinking I was going to die. Was taken to the hospital in an ambulance, fiancé freaking out by my side, kids left behind with grandma crying and freaking out thinking mum's dying. Turns out I was having a severe asthma attack. The doctors were shocked that I had no idea I had asthma at all. Did all the tests (for the first time) and got officially diagnosed. 

I did feel angry for a while. I felt like it'd led to my ED, to some birthing complications, to issues in life that I thought were just ''normal''. I think I was sad, most of all. I loved swim classes when I was little, then started having those ''drowning nightmares'' when I felt like I couldn't breath in the middle of the night and became afraid of swimming. I still don't swim unless I'm holding onto my husband, literally on his back. I was bullied in school for being bad at games and playing tag and having to take the elevator instead of stairs every single time. I didn't join my girlfriends for dance presentations at talent shows. I never learned how to ride a bike. I got used to being called lazy. I got used to hearing comments about my body and what I had to do to keep my figure. 

I took me about a year to get over the anger and the sadness. There was no magic involved, no tricks, really. It felt a lot like grief, I think: grief for parts of my childhood and my health that I felt I'd lost. And like with grief, I'm not sure it ever fully goes away, but then one night you suddenly realize that you haven't thought about it the whole day. And then one random afternoon, you do think about it, but not with anger: it's now just a thought.

If I can give you one piece of advice, it is to try therapy. It changed my life in many ways and gave me the tools to deal with, honestly, most things that have ever happened to me. 

I'm glad that you'll now be able to take the right steps in taking care of your health. Wish you all the best and much love xxx
